summary:
Ayacucho stands under Peru's national framework. No region-specific trans statute, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding for the department appears in the sources, and all three attached sources are national in scope, so the operative facts for a visitor are the national ones.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but public-facility access is now restricted by law. Bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante, were approved unanimously by the congressional Women and Family Commission on 20 February 2025 and the merged dictamen was approved by the plenary and exempted from second vote on 2 April 2025. Its article 5 bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their biological sex, with exceptions only for custody, where medical attention is required, or for accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities; the same package bans 'ambiguous' bathroom signage. The legislative trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at the Jorge Chávez airport.

The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents carries the same rule into force for trans people, including trans youth, and bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Enforcement reaches private premises as well as state facilities: a consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that applied the policy. Whether the 2 April 2025 bill has formally entered into force is not documented in the attached sources, and if it is in force a trans traveller using public restrooms in Ayacucho faces a live national legal exposure.

Practical access depends on front-line discretion. LGTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho warns that restroom use would come to depend on security staff's personal judgment, including identity checks, and notes there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

Hate-crime protection is absent. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, and violence against trans people is documented and rising: 54 TLGBI people were killed and 170 rights-violation cases recorded over 2020-2023, with trans women more than half the homicide victims at 30, against 23 gay men and one lesbian. Killings rose to 19 in 2023, 12 of them trans women, from 13 in 2022, 10 in 2021 and 12 in 2020, many committed with cruelty. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected.

One case defines the ceiling of protection. In February 2023 the trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano, 31, was abducted by a gang in central Lima and killed in Carabayllo with about 30 gunshots as part of an extortion scheme.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in an analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, concludes that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, and that the stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype presenting trans people as likely restroom harassers, while UN reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

IDEHPUCP also found the bathroom provision openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity and implicitly framing them as harassment risks, and recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Hostility extends to public speech. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Speech and association are constrained by the same legislative package. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years; Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Comparatively, the 2017 repeal left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.
localsOnly:
Two protective developments are on record for residents. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack and after years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history; the case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The 2017 repeal was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures.

The 170 rights-violation cases recorded over 2020-2023 include state violence and incitement to discrimination, with 61 denuncias filed in 2020 alone.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the bill approved by the plenary on 2 April 2025 has entered into force is not documented in the attached sources; the sources record committee approval in February 2025 and plenary approval with exemption from second vote in April 2025, and no commencement date.

No source in the inventory addresses Ayacucho directly. There is no departmental record of restroom enforcement, of complaints brought under the April 2025 law, of regional health-service practice after the June 2024 terminology change, or of incidents of violence against trans people in the department; the homicide and violation figures are national with no sub-national breakdown.

The recorded hate-crime and homicide figures are acknowledged by their own co-author, the trans journalist and human-rights defender Gianna Camacho, to be a sub-registry rather than a complete count, so the true level of violence is not established by these sources.

The dismissal of a trans woman's complaint against a gym is a single national consumer-protection decision; its treatment of equivalent complaints in Ayacucho is not sourced.
